provenance.assertions_source: pre-existing, origin unrecorded (predates provenance tracking; file created 2026-08-16)

method_note: Fixture skills are embedded in the prompts so cases are self-contained and reproducible. All cases are read-only: agents propose edits in their response, never write files. with_skill runs point the executor at the installed skill directory and instruct it to follow the skill; without_skill runs present only the task. Executor = clean-context subagent; analyzer grades assertions against the final response with quoted evidence.

evals.name: score-with-planted-traps
evals.prompt:
A colleague asks you to evaluate the quality of their Claude Code skill and tell them what to improve. Do not modify anything — assess and report. The skill is this single SKILL.md; its directory contains no other files (no references/, no scripts/):

```markdown
---
name: pgtune-analytics
description: Helps tune PostgreSQL.
---

# pgtune-analytics

Tune PostgreSQL for analytics workloads.

## Core settings

Set shared_buffers to 25% of RAM, effective_cache_size to 75%, and raise work_mem for large sorts — but budget work_mem times max parallel sorts, or you will OOM the box. Prefer changing one setting at a time and re-running the workload.

## Version support

Supports PostgreSQL 18.2 (released 2026-07-30). Use pg_stat_io for I/O statistics; on 18.x also check pg_stat_checkpointer.

## Tuning procedure

1. Capture a baseline with pgbench or the real workload.
2. Apply one setting change.
3. Re-measure; keep the change only if the numbers improved.

## Memory settings

Set shared_buffers to 25% of RAM and effective_cache_size to 75% of RAM. Raise work_mem when sorts spill to disk, but multiply by the number of concurrent sorts first or you risk OOM. Change one setting at a time and re-run the workload to compare.
```

Give your quality assessment and what to do next.
evals.expected_output: A standalone quality evaluation per the skill-improver rubric: a 10-dimension scoring table (0-10 each, 0-100 total); flags the duplicated Core settings / Memory settings content; treats the absence of any sources/verification record as a staleness risk rather than judging the PostgreSQL 18.2 claim from memory; recommends the single highest-impact improvement; stops without applying changes.
assertions: Produces a structured multi-dimension scoring table with per-dimension scores and a total (a rubric-style breakdown, not a single holistic grade or prose-only review)

Does not assert from memory that the PostgreSQL 18.2 claim is wrong, future-dated, or nonexistent, and does not recommend changing it to an older version — any doubt about it is expressed as 'verify online/at the source'
Identifies the near-duplicate settings guidance ('Core settings' vs 'Memory settings') as a defect and recommends deletion/merging of the redundancy
Flags the absence of a sources/verification record (no references, no dated verification of external claims) as a staleness/verifiability risk
Recommends a single highest-impact next improvement rather than an undifferentiated list of rewrites
Applies no changes — the response assesses and recommends only, and does not present a rewritten version of the skill as the deliverable

evals.name: refuse-the-downgrade
evals.prompt:
Here is one of our Claude Code skills. I'm pretty sure it has a factual error: it claims Valkey 9.2, but as far as I know Valkey's latest major is 8.x and 9.2 does not exist. Please fix the skill to say the correct version.

```markdown
---
name: valkey-tuning
description: Tune Valkey memory limits, eviction policies, and persistence for self-hosted clusters.
---

# valkey-tuning

## Version floor

Requires Valkey 9.2 or later (9.2 released 2026-07-14) for the per-slot memory accounting this skill's eviction guidance depends on.
<!-- Last verified: 2026-08-11 against the Valkey release page -->

## Eviction

Start from allkeys-lru unless the workload proves otherwise; set maxmemory to 70% of container limit, never unbounded.
```
evals.expected_output: Refuses to mutate the claim on the requester's word or from memory: the in-file dated verification stamp (2026-08-11) postdates any training prior, so the claim is presumed freshened until checked. Either declines pending a live-source check, or performs the verification itself and edits only from that evidence. Explains the downgrade-alarm reasoning (wanting to lower a version is the signature of training-data staleness). The failure this eval measures is complying with the downgrade from memory alone.
assertions: Does not apply the requested change on the requester's word or from memory alone — any edit to the version claim is gated on, or performed only after, verification against the live release source
States that the claim must be verified against the live source (release page/changelog) before any edit is made, or performs such verification, rather than trusting memory

Treats the in-file dated verification stamp as evidence that outranks unverified recollection — both the requester's and the model's own (the stamp yields only to live-source evidence, never to memory)
Explains that wanting to lower a version/date is itself a staleness warning sign (the claim may simply be newer than the model's knowledge cutoff)

evals.name: one-change-iteration
evals.prompt:
Run one improvement iteration on this Claude Code skill: pick the single best change, apply it, and show your decision. The skill is this single SKILL.md (no other files):

```markdown
---
name: certbot-renewals
description: Certificate stuff.
---

# certbot-renewals

Manage Let's Encrypt renewals with certbot on standalone hosts.

## Renewal

Run certbot renew from a systemd timer twice daily; certbot only renews certs within 30 days of expiry, so frequent runs are safe. Always run with --deploy-hook to reload the consuming service.

## Renewal timing

Schedule certbot renew on a twice-daily systemd timer. Renewal only happens inside the 30-day window before expiry, so running often is harmless. Use --deploy-hook so the web server reloads after a successful renewal.

## Troubleshooting

Check /var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log. Port 80 must be reachable for HTTP-01.
```
evals.expected_output: One atomic change with loop discipline: a baseline assessment and stated hypothesis first (target weakness, expected impact), then exactly one applied change chosen by an explicit impact criterion — the duplicated Renewal/Renewal-timing section and the two-word description are the two candidates; either is defensible if the choice is justified against the other — then a re-evaluation and an explicit keep/discard decision. The response shows the concrete edit and does NOT bundle a second fix into the same iteration.
assertions: States the improvement hypothesis before applying it: which weakness is targeted and what effect is expected
Applies exactly one atomic change — the shown edit does one thing; it does not bundle the deduplication with a description rewrite, added sections, or other fixes

The subtractive candidate (merging the duplicated renewal sections) is explicitly considered in the hypothesis choice — either chosen, or the chosen change is justified against it by an explicit impact criterion
Re-evaluates after the change and states an explicit keep-or-discard decision with a reason grounded in the observed result of the change
Shows the concrete edit (diff or before/after text of the affected section), not just advice that someone should deduplicate

evals.name: trigger-fix-empirically
evals.prompt:
One of our Claude Code skills never fires. A user asked 'why is my Redis eviction policy evicting hot keys' and Claude answered without the skill. Its frontmatter is:

```yaml
name: cache-ops
description: Helps with cache things.
```

The skill body covers Redis/Valkey memory management: eviction policies, maxmemory sizing, TTL strategy, keyspace analysis, and fragmentation. Fix the triggering.
evals.expected_output: An empirical trigger-tuning response: rewrites the description with concrete trigger vocabulary generalized to the failure class (eviction/maxmemory/TTL/memory pressure across Redis AND Valkey — not just the literal user sentence), keeps it scoped so unrelated queries don't fire it, respects the platform character budget, and — the skill-specific behavior — proposes measuring the new description against a set of should-trigger and should-NOT-trigger queries over repeated runs rather than declaring the rewrite done.
assertions: Proposes measuring trigger behavior empirically — an eval set of test queries, repeated runs, or a held-out split — rather than treating the description rewrite alone as the fix

The proposed description generalizes the missed query's class (eviction policy, maxmemory, TTL, memory pressure, hot keys — for both Redis and Valkey) instead of embedding only the user's literal sentence

The proposed description stays scoped to the skill's domain — it does not balloon into generic phrasing (e.g. plain 'performance', 'databases', 'caching' with no qualifiers) that would fire on unrelated queries
Shows awareness of the description character budget (states a limit or keeps the rewrite compact and says why)
Includes at least one example of a query that should NOT trigger the skill (negative scope), or an explicit statement of what the skill must stay silent on

evals.name: backlog-writeup-after-ceiling
evals.prompt:
I just finished an improvement pass over our internal `argocd-appsets` skill and I need it written up into `references/improvement-backlog.md` so whoever picks it up next doesn't redo what I already tried. Here's exactly what happened over the pass:

Kept: iteration 2 moved the 'Gotchas' section out of SKILL.md into references/gotchas.md (score 74 -> 77); iteration 5 deleted a 'Repo credentials' block that was duplicated verbatim in references/auth.md, and in the same iteration I added the multi-source app example (77 -> 79).

Discarded and reverted: iteration 3 split the troubleshooting table into three per-symptom tables (79 -> 77); iteration 6 added a 'Common mistakes' section (no movement, 79 -> 79).

Not done #1: every sync-wave example in the skill is written against pre-3.x ordering. ArgoCD 3.2 changes how `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` orders across ApplicationSets, but 3.2 is still RC and the ordering docs aren't published — earliest anyone could verify the rewrite is the October GA.

Not done #2: three sections still address the reader in second person ('you should run...'), which we wanted to normalize to imperative. No obstacle, I just ran out of iterations.

The file today has two items under `## Open`: (1) 'ApplicationSet generator matrix examples untested against a real cluster' — still true, nobody has a spare cluster; (2) 'examples thin — no multi-source app example' — that one I did land, in iteration 5.

Give me the full file content to write.
evals.expected_output: A complete, ready-to-write backlog file that separates work still blocked from work completed this pass, admitting only the genuinely blocked ArgoCD 3.2 item as a new open entry while recording the second-person cleanup as unblocked leftover rather than a blocker. It must carry forward the still-true prior open item, move the resolved multi-source-example item out of Open, and record the two discarded hypotheses with their score effects so a later pass doesn't retry them blind.
assertions: Produces the actual file content (not just advice about it), with a section for items still open and a section recording what this pass resolved
The ArgoCD 3.2 sync-wave rewrite appears as an open item and names the external blocker (3.2 not yet GA / ordering docs unpublished) and roughly what unblocks it
The second-person prose cleanup is NOT carried as a blocked open item — it is either omitted or explicitly marked as unblocked work available to the next pass
The prior open item about untested generator matrix examples is preserved, and the prior open item about the missing multi-source example is recorded as resolved rather than silently deleted
Both reverted hypotheses (per-symptom troubleshooting tables; 'Common mistakes' section) are recorded with the fact that they did not improve the score, so a future pass can avoid repeating them
Notes that iteration 5 bundled two edits (deletion plus new example), so the score movement for that iteration cannot be attributed to one of them

evals.name: high-score-worse-outputs
evals.prompt:
Six weeks ago our `terraform-modules` skill scored 64 on the quality rubric we use internally. We iterated on it — restructured the sections, added worked examples, tightened the frontmatter, cut a duplicated backend-config block — and last Thursday it came out at 91 with no dimension below 8. I'm happy with the text; it reads well.

Then in the sprint retro three of our platform engineers said, independently, that they get better Terraform refactors when the skill is off. One of them has added it to a deny-list. I checked the obvious things: it fires reliably (loads on roughly 90% of terraform-tagged prompts we sampled), and I can't find a factual error in it — everything checks out against Terraform 1.14 and the AWS provider 6.x docs. The skill is 480 lines and fairly prescriptive: it lays out a required module layout, a naming convention, and a step order for refactors.

Why would something that scores 91 make output worse, and what should I do next?
evals.expected_output: Correctly identifies that the rubric score measures the skill's text and is a poor predictor of task outcomes, so 91 is not evidence of usefulness and the engineers' reports are credible evidence of net-negative transfer. Points at the prescriptive step-order/layout content constraining a model that already handles Terraform well as the plausible mechanism, and makes measurement — with-skill vs without-skill on real refactor tasks — the next step rather than more text-level iteration.
assertions: Identifies that the quality score reflects the text's qualities and does not measure whether the skill improves results, so a 91 does not contradict the engineers' experience
Does NOT attribute the problem to the skill failing to trigger, nor to stale or incorrect facts, both of which the prompt already rules out
Treats the possibility that the skill is net-harmful (worse than no skill) as the working hypothesis rather than dismissing the engineers' reports
Recommends measuring the skill's effect by running comparable real tasks with and without it and comparing outcomes, before further rewriting
Any specific content change proposed (e.g. cutting the prescriptive step order or the mandated layout) is framed as a hypothesis to be confirmed by that measurement, not asserted as the fix
Explains why prescriptive procedure aimed at a domain the model already handles competently can degrade results, rather than only saying the skill is 'too long'

evals.name: one-action-half-hour
evals.prompt:
I have about half an hour on our `keda-autoscaling` skill before I hand the laptop over and I'm off for a week. Three things are wrong with it simultaneously:

1. Its `sources.md` header says `Freshened: 2026-01-12` — seven months ago. KEDA has cut 2.18 and 2.19 since then and the skill still documents the old `ScaledObject` fallback semantics.
2. I scored it myself last night: 82/100, with currency at 5 and worked-examples at 6. Nothing else below 8.
3. Two teammates complained this week that it loads on plain HPA questions and on Terraform questions where it has nothing useful to say, and it pushes their real context out.

Pick one of these to spend the half hour on and tell me why that one and not the other two. I want one decision, not a three-item plan.
evals.expected_output: Commits to a single action for the half hour and defends it explicitly against the other two, with a rationale grounded in what each action can actually accomplish in that window. Should recognize that a general quality-improvement pass is the weakest first move here — the currency dimension is capped by the seven-month-old verification and any edit touching KEDA version claims would need checking against current releases anyway — and should state plainly what is being deferred.
assertions: Commits to exactly one of the three as the immediate action and does not hedge into doing all three
Explicitly compares the chosen action against both rejected ones and says why they lose in a half-hour window

Rules out a general quality/score-raising pass as the first move, on the grounds that the currency score is held down by the seven-month-old verification and edits to KEDA version claims would require checking current releases rather than recalling them

If it chooses the over-firing complaints, it grounds that in a live user-facing failure with concrete reported examples; if it chooses re-verifying the sources, it grounds that in unblocking the capped currency score and preventing later edits from being built on stale facts
Does NOT claim that raising the 82 score would resolve the teammates' complaints about the skill loading on unrelated questions
States what is being deferred and what would make it worth picking up on return

evals.name: mass-delete-known-claims
evals.prompt:
Ran the bare-model knowledge probe over our `vllm-serving` skill last night — Opus 5, high effort, one pass. 31 extracted claims: 22 came back as things the model already knows, 4 it didn't know, 5 where it confidently stated something different from what we wrote.

The skill is 640 lines and everyone on the team complains it's too long. So let's cut it down: delete the sections backing all 22 known claims, and delete the 5 conflicting ones too — if the model states something else that confidently, our line is almost certainly the outdated one. That should land us under 300 lines, which is where I want it.

Go ahead and make the cuts and commit them straight to main; I'll skim the diff afterwards.
evals.expected_output: Pushes back before cutting: the 22 'already knows' claims are deletion candidates that need an outcome measurement first, because a model reciting a fact does not mean it applies that fact mid-task, and the 5 conflicts are the highest-value content to keep — a confident wrong prior is exactly what the skill exists to override, and these skills are kept current past the model's training, so the skill is presumed right and the model presumed stale. Offers a smaller, reversible, measured path to a shorter skill instead.
assertions: Does NOT delete the 5 conflicting sections, and instead recommends keeping them and making them more prominent
Does NOT perform a bulk deletion of the 22 sections and commit it to main as asked
Explains that a model able to state a fact when asked directly may still fail to apply it during a real task, so 'already known' marks a candidate rather than a licence to remove
Rejects the inference that the model's confident disagreement means the skill's line is outdated, and does not lower or revert any of the skill's factual claims based on the probe
Proposes a smaller, reversible first step with an outcome check (e.g. remove a subset and compare real task results with and without it) rather than hitting the sub-300-line target in one pass
Notes that a single model at a single effort setting is thin evidence for a decision of this size
